params.name: sourceFile
params.javadoc: the source file or directory to be copied. It must not be `null`.

params.name: destinationDirectory
params.javadoc: the destination directory where the source file or directory will be copied to. It must not be `null`. It is created only after every argument has been validated, so a rejected call never leaves a new directory behind.

params.name: preserveFileDate
params.javadoc: if `true`, the last modified date of the file will be preserved in the copied file.

params.name: filter
params.type: Throwables.BiPredicate<? super File, ? super File, E>
params.javadoc: a BiPredicate that takes the source directory and the file being evaluated as arguments and returns a boolean. If the predicate returns `true`, the file is copied; if it returns `false`, the file is not copied. It selects the source's contents and is never asked about `sourceFile` itself, so a plain-file source is copied whatever the filter answers (the same convention as #deleteFilesFromDirectory(File, Throwables.BiPredicate)). A rejected subdirectory is still descended into, so that its own matching entries are copied - which means the destination mirrors the source's directory structure in full, including directories that ended up holding nothing.

if `sourceFile` does not exist, cannot be read, or is neither a file nor a directory.

if listing or reading `sourceDirectory`, creating `destinationDirectory` or its descendants, or copying their contents fails, if the source directory does not exist or cannot be read (a FileNotFoundException), if its contents cannot be listed — which is reported rather than mistaken for an empty directory, so a normal return always means the whole source was copied — or if a copied file's timestamp cannot be applied.

methods.javadoc_summary: Copies the contents of a directory to another directory.
contract: If the destination directory does not exist, it is created.

`destinationDirectory` must not be `sourceDirectory` itself, nor lie inside it: the copy would keep finding the entries it had just written.
Last-modified times are preserved, as in #copyToDirectory(File, File): the copy fails after writing a file's bytes if its last-modified time cannot be applied.

methods.javadoc_summary: Copies a file to a new location preserving the file date.
contract: The directory holding the destination file is created if it does not exist.
If the destination file exists, then this method overwrites it.
Whether an existing read-only destination is replaced is platform-defined: POSIX replaces the entry when its directory is writable, Windows refuses with an `AccessDeniedException`.
If the modification operation fails, it falls back to File#setLastModified(long), and if that fails, the method throws IOException.
This method preserves the source's last-modified time (failing if it cannot) and attempts to preserve the other file times too.

methods.name: copyFile
methods.signature: public static void copyFile(final File sourceFile, final File destinationFile, final boolean preserveFileDate) throws IllegalArgumentException, IOException

params.name: sourceFile
params.javadoc: an existing file to copy, must not be `null`.

params.name: destinationFile
params.javadoc: the new file, must not be `null`.

params.name: preserveFileDate
params.javadoc: `true` to apply the source's last-modified time (and, best effort, its other file times) to the copy, failing if the last-modified time cannot be applied; `false` to skip that step. methods.javadoc_summary: Deletes the specified file and all its subfiles/directories recursively if it's a directory.
methods.returns: `true` if the file/directory and all its contents were deleted successfully; `false` if the file is `null`, does not exist (and is not a dangling symbolic link), or any part of it could not be deleted (in which case part of the tree may already be gone).
contract: If the specified file is a directory, it will delete all files and subdirectories within it before deleting the directory itself.
If the file is a regular file, it will simply delete the file.
If the file does not exist or is `null`, the method returns `false` without performing any operations.

Usage Examples: Deletion is best-effort and not transactional: every entry is attempted, one that cannot be removed does not stop the rest of the tree, and `false` is returned at the end if any of them failed - so a `false` result normally means the tree was partially removed rather than left untouched.
That includes a dangling link handed in directly: File#exists() answers `false` for one, but it is not "absent" here - the link itself is removed, exactly as it would be when met inside a tree.

A path ending in `"."` names the directory itself (`x/.` is `x`); one ending in `".."` names the directory's parent - the tree ABOVE the one spelled - and is rejected as a bad argument rather than acted on, as #renameTo(File, String) rejects it as a name - also when trailing `"."` elements follow the `".."` (`x/../.`, `x/../../.`), since those fold onto the parent too.
On Windows a trailing element made only of dots and spaces (`"..."`) names the directory before it, as `"."` does, and is likewise ignored when deciding (`x/../...` is rejected too).

Deletion is best-effort and not transactional: every entry is attempted, and `false` is returned at the end if any of them failed, so a `false` result normally means the tree was partially deleted.
`false` is also the answer when the protection above kicks in.

A path ending in `"."` names the directory itself (`x/.` is `x`); one ending in `".."` names the directory's parent and is rejected as a bad argument rather than acted on, as by #deleteRecursivelyIfExists(File) - also when trailing `"."` elements follow the `".."` (`x/../.`), since those fold onto the parent too.

methods.javadoc_summary: Tests whether the contents of two files are equal.

types.name: IdentityHashSet
types.javadoc_summary: A Set implementation that uses reference-equality (==) instead of object-equality (equals()) when comparing elements.

constructors.signature: public IdentityHashSet()
constructors.javadoc_summary: Constructs a new, empty identity hash set with the default initial capacity of the backing IdentityHashMap.
examples: IdentityHashSet<Object> set = new IdentityHashSet<>();

constructors.signature: public IdentityHashSet(final int initialCapacity) throws IllegalArgumentException
constructors.javadoc_summary: Constructs a new, empty identity hash set sized to hold approximately the specified number of elements.

params.name: initialCapacity
params.javadoc: the initial capacity of the identity hash set

throws.condition: if the initial capacity is negative.

examples: IdentityHashSet<String> set = new IdentityHashSet<>(100);

constructors.signature: public IdentityHashSet(final Collection<? extends T> c)
constructors.javadoc_summary: Constructs a new identity hash set containing the elements in the specified collection.

params.name: c
params.javadoc: the collection whose elements are to be placed into this set; a `null` collection results in an empty set

examples:
List<String> list = Arrays.asList("a", "b", "c");
IdentityHashSet<String> set = new IdentityHashSet<>(list);

methods.name: add
methods.signature: @Override public boolean add(final T e)

params.name: e
params.javadoc: element to be added to this set

methods.javadoc_summary: Adds the specified element to this set if it is not already present using reference-equality comparison.
methods.returns: `true` if this set did not already contain the specified element
contract: More formally, adds the specified element e to this set if the set contains no element e2 such that (e==e2).

methods.name: remove
methods.signature: @Override public boolean remove(final Object o)

params.name: o
params.javadoc: object to be removed from this set, if present

methods.javadoc_summary: Removes the specified element from this set if it is present using reference-equality comparison.
methods.returns: `true` if the set contained the specified element
contract: More formally, removes an element e such that (o==e), if this set contains such an element.

methods.name: containsAll
methods.signature: @Override public boolean containsAll(final Collection<?> c)

params.name: c
params.javadoc: collection to be checked for containment in this set; `null` is treated as empty

methods.javadoc_summary: Returns `true` if this set contains all of the elements in the specified collection.
methods.returns: `true` if this set contains all of the elements in the specified collection; `true` if `c` is `null` or empty

methods.name: addAll
methods.signature: @Override public boolean addAll(final Collection<? extends T> c)

params.name: c
params.javadoc: collection containing elements to be added to this set; `null` is treated as empty

methods.javadoc_summary: Adds all of the elements in the specified collection to this set using reference-equality comparison.
methods.returns: `true` if this set changed as a result of the call
contract: For each element e in the collection, it is added if the set contains no element e2 such that (e==e2).

methods.name: removeAll
methods.signature: @Override public boolean removeAll(final Collection<?> c)

params.name: c
params.javadoc: collection containing elements to be removed from this set; `null` is treated as empty

methods.javadoc_summary: Removes from this set all of its elements that are contained in the specified collection using reference-equality comparison.
methods.returns: `true` if this set changed as a result of the call

methods.name: retainAll
methods.signature: @Override public boolean retainAll(final Collection<?> c)

params.name: c
params.javadoc: collection containing elements to be retained in this set; `null` is treated as empty, which clears this set

methods.javadoc_summary: Retains only the elements in this set that are contained in the specified collection using reference-equality comparison.
methods.returns: `true` if this set changed as a result of the call

methods.name: contains
methods.signature: @Override public boolean contains(final Object valueToFind)

params.name: valueToFind
params.javadoc: element whose presence in this set is to be tested

methods.javadoc_summary: Returns `true` if this set contains the specified element using reference-equality comparison.
methods.returns: `true` if this set contains the specified element based on reference equality
contract: More formally, returns `true` if and only if this set contains an element e such that (valueToFind==e).

methods.name: iterator
methods.signature: @Override public Iterator<T> iterator()
methods.javadoc_summary: Returns an iterator over the elements in this set.
methods.returns: an iterator over the elements in this set
contract: The iterator is fail-fast on a best-effort basis: structural modification outside the iterator after its creation will generally cause a java.util.ConcurrentModificationException, but this must not be relied on for correctness.

methods.name: toArray
methods.signature: @Override public Object[] toArray()

methods.returns: an array containing all of the elements in this set

methods.signature: @Override public <A> A[] toArray(final A[] a) throws NullPointerException, ArrayStoreException

params.name: a
params.javadoc: the array into which the elements of this set are to be stored, if it is big enough; otherwise, a new array of the same runtime type is allocated

throws.condition: if `a` is `null`
if the runtime type of the specified array is not a supertype of the runtime type of every element in this set

methods.javadoc_summary: Returns an array containing all of the elements in this set; the runtime type of the returned array is that of the specified array.
methods.returns: an array containing all of the elements in this set
contract: If the set fits in the specified array, it is returned therein.

methods.name: size
methods.signature: @Override public int size()
methods.javadoc_summary: Returns the number of elements in this set (its cardinality).
methods.returns: the number of elements in this set

methods.name: isEmpty
methods.signature: @Override public boolean isEmpty()
methods.javadoc_summary: Returns `true` if this set contains no elements.
methods.returns: `true` if this set contains no elements

methods.name: clear
methods.signature: @Override public void clear()
methods.javadoc_summary: Removes all of the elements from this set.

methods.name: equals
methods.signature: @SuppressWarnings("rawtypes") @Override public boolean equals(final Object o)

params.name: o
params.javadoc: object to be compared for equality with this set

methods.javadoc_summary: Compares the specified object with this set for equality using reference (identity) semantics.
methods.returns: `true` if `o` is an `IdentityHashSet` containing exactly the same object references as this set; `false` otherwise
contract: Returns `true` only if the specified object is also an `IdentityHashSet` and the two sets contain the exact same object references (compared with `==`).
A non-`IdentityHashSet` (for example a java.util.HashSet) is never considered equal to this set, even if they appear to contain the same elements by `equals`.

methods.javadoc_summary: Returns a hash code for this set: the sum of System#identityHashCode(Object) of each element (as defined by `IdentityHashMap`'s key-set view).
methods.returns: the hash code value for this set

methods.signature: @Override public String toString()
methods.javadoc_summary: Returns a string representation of this set.
methods.returns: a string representation of this set

The copy is skipped only when `map` is an `ImmutableBiMap` that already owns its backing storage - one produced by `of(...)`, `copyOf(...)`, #empty() or the no-arg #builder(), or the #inverse() of such a map.

The map's values must be unique, as required by BiMap; the entries are inserted in the source's iteration order, so which entry is reported as the offender for a duplicate value depends on that order.
An `ImmutableBiMap` source is copied through its own backing-map suppliers, which reproduce it exactly only when they build the same kind of map that backs it.
Build the entries into a `BiMap` whose backing maps you chose and call #wrap(BiMap) (or #copyOf(BiMap)) when a particular order must be guaranteed.

If the source is a SortedMap, the returned map uses the same java.util.Comparator (or natural ordering) as the source, even when the source is empty.
Wrap the view in a fresh map (`copyOf(new TreeMap<>(view))`) when a small view of a large map must stop retaining it.

methods.javadoc_summary: Returns an ImmutableNavigableSet containing the elements of the specified collection.
methods.returns: an `ImmutableNavigableSet` containing the elements of the specified collection, or the same instance if it is already an `ImmutableNavigableSet` that owns its backing storage. The comparator of a `SortedSet` source is retained even when the source is empty; a `null` or empty non-sorted source returns the shared empty instance.
contract: If the provided collection is already an instance of ImmutableNavigableSet that owns its backing storage (one produced by `of(...)`, `copyOf(...)` or #empty()), it is directly returned; a #wrap(NavigableSet)-created view is copied like any other collection.
If the provided collection is `null` or empty, an empty ImmutableNavigableSet is returned.
A SortedSet source retains its comparator, including when it is empty; its elements need not implement Comparable when that comparator supports them.
Other collections use natural ordering and throw ClassCastException if their elements are not mutually comparable.
Wrap the view in a fresh set (`copyOf(new TreeSet<>(view))`) when a small view of a large source must stop retaining it.

Index.last(arr, 5.0f, 3, 0.1f).isPresent();             // returns false

methods.javadoc_summary: Compares this Indexed instance to the specified object for equality.
methods.returns: `true` if the specified object is equal to this Indexed instance, `false` otherwise.
contract: Returns `true` if and only if the specified object is also an Indexed instance, and both instances have the same index and equal values.
Two Indexed instances are equal if they have the same index (primitive long comparison) and equal values.

This implementation follows the general contract of Object#equals(Object): Reflexive: `x.equals(x)` returns `true` Symmetric: `x.equals(y)` returns `true` if and only if `y.equals(x)` returns `true` Transitive: If `x.equals(y)` and `y.equals(z)`, then `x.equals(z)` Consistent: Multiple invocations return the same result (assuming no modification) Null comparison: `x.equals(null)` returns `false` Usage Examples:

contract: Discovering a custom constructor does not invoke it; if a constructor later fails for a requested capacity, the returned function throws an IllegalArgumentException with the constructor failure as its cause - except that an `IllegalArgumentException` from N#newInstance(Class) (the path of a class whose `(int)` constructor is absent or not used), including one thrown by the constructor itself, is rethrown unchanged.
Such a class is created the way Suppliers#ofCollection(Class) creates it, which rejects it with an IllegalArgumentException when it has no usable construction path.
Register an explicit creator before the first factory lookup when that argument is not a capacity.
A registered creator must return an instance of `targetType` itself, and readers do not use it (see N#newInstance(Class)).

methods.name: defer

params.name: iteratorSupplier
params.javadoc: a `Supplier` that provides the `IntIterator` when needed

throws.condition: if `iteratorSupplier` is `null`.

methods.javadoc_summary: Creates a deferred IntIterator that is initialized lazily using the provided Supplier.
methods.returns: a lazily initialized `IntIterator`
contract: If it throws a runtime exception or error, that same failure is cached and rethrown by subsequent access attempts.
Its access methods throw IllegalStateException if the supplier returns `null` or recursively accesses this iterator during initialization.
Initialization exceptions and errors are cached and rethrown on later access, even if the supplier catches a recursive-access failure.
The supplier must return a valid source distinct from this deferred iterator and must not create a cycle through other delegating iterators.

methods.name: min
methods.signature: public static OptionalChar min(final char... a)

params.name: a
params.javadoc: the array of characters to evaluate.

methods.javadoc_summary: Returns the minimum value from the provided array of characters.
methods.returns: an `OptionalChar` containing the minimum value if the array is not `null` or empty, otherwise an empty `OptionalChar`.
contract: If the array is `null` or empty, it returns an empty `OptionalChar`.

Usage Examples: Note: a bare `Iterables.min()` is ambiguous among the seven primitive overloads, and `Iterables.min(null)` is ambiguous among the reference overloads (#min(Iterable), #min(Iterator) and #min(Comparable[])); pass a typed empty array or a typed `null` (for example `min(new char[0])` or `min((char[]) null)`) when the element type is not implied by the arguments.
examples:
char[] array = {'a', 'b', 'c'};
OptionalChar result = Iterables.min(array);   // OptionalChar[a]

if reached elements cannot be compared using the selected ordering.

methods.javadoc_summary: Returns the minimum value from the provided iterator of elements according to the provided comparator.
methods.returns: a `Nullable` containing the minimum value if the iterator is not `null` or empty, otherwise an empty `Nullable`.
contract: If the iterator is `null` or empty, it returns an empty `Nullable`.

When `comparator` is the nulls-first comparator - the one shared instance returned by both Comparators#nullsFirst() and Comparators#naturalOrder() - nothing can compare less than `null`, so this method returns after a comparison leaves a null running candidate, leaving the remaining elements unread.
If the first element is null, a second element is still consumed when available before this check.
examples:
Iterator<String> iter = Arrays.asList("b", "a", "c").iterator();
Nullable<String> result = Iterables.min(iter, Comparator.reverseOrder());   // Nullable[c]

contract: If the provided iterable is empty, an empty iterator will be returned.
If the number of rounds is zero, an empty iterator will be returned.

Structural modification of the source is governed by that collection's own iterator contract: a fail-fast collection raises java.util.ConcurrentModificationException, while one whose iterator does not fail fast picks up the change on the next round - and, if the source has been emptied, ends the iteration early instead of walking the remaining rounds.
Note: when `rounds > 0`, `iterable.iterator()` is obtained eagerly, when this method is called.
When `rounds == 0`, no iterator is obtained at all.

params.name: c

throws.condition: if `size` is negative, or if `c` is empty or `null` when `size > 0`.

methods.javadoc_summary: Repeats the entire specified Collection cyclically until the specified total size is reached.
methods.returns: an `ObjIterator` that cycles through the collection until `size` elements have been produced.
contract: The collection is repeated as a whole, cycling through it multiple times if necessary.

If the source is emptied and its iterator does not fail fast, the next `next()` throws NoSuchElementException even though `hasNext()` reported `true`, because the requested `size` can no longer be produced.

methods.javadoc_summary: Performs an action for each selected element of the given iterator, using the slicing and processing configuration carried by the supplied IterateOptions.
contract: When `processThreads > 0`, this method creates a new dedicated thread pool for this call and shuts it down before returning.

methods.javadoc_summary: Returns the compensated sum of all added values.
methods.returns: the sum with Kahan error compensation applied
contract: If the result is NaN and the simple sum is infinite, returns the simple sum instead.

Unlike #average(), this method has no overflow-safe fallback: once the running sum of finite values overflows, the result stays infinite even if later values cancel the excess, so it can depend on the order in which the values were added.

If only the compensated total overflows while the plain running sum stays finite, the result is `NaN` even though every value is finite: `KahanSummation.of(Double.MAX_VALUE, 0x1p969, 0x1p969).sum()` returns `NaN`, as java.util.DoubleSummaryStatistics#getSum() does for the same values.

methods.name: invert
methods.signature: public ListMultimap<E, K> invert()
methods.javadoc_summary: Inverts the ListMultimap, swapping keys with values.
methods.returns: a new instance of ListMultimap where the original keys are now values and the original values are now keys
contract: If multiple keys in the original multimap share the same value, that value will be associated with multiple keys in the inverted multimap.
The returned multimap's backing map is a HashMap when this multimap's backing map is exactly a `HashMap`, and otherwise a java.util.LinkedHashMap that preserves this multimap's encounter order.

The original backing class - sorted, identity, concurrent, weak or custom - is never mirrored, because its key handling (a comparator, reference equivalence, thread safety, weak keys) applies to the original keys, not to the inverted ones: a sorted multimap does not invert into a sorted one, and a java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap-backed one does not invert into a concurrent one - unlike #copy(), which reuses this multimap's map supplier, or the kind of its backing map when it has no map supplier.

types.name: LongList
types.javadoc_summary: A high-performance, resizable array implementation for primitive long values that provides specialized operations optimized for 64-bit integer data types.

constructors.signature: public LongList()
constructors.javadoc_summary: Constructs an empty LongList with an initial capacity of zero.
examples:
LongList list = new LongList();
list.size();     // returns 0
list.isEmpty();  // returns true
list.add(1L);    // list is now [1]

constructors.signature: public LongList(final int initialCapacity) throws IllegalArgumentException, OutOfMemoryError
constructors.javadoc_summary: Constructs an empty LongList with the specified initial capacity.

params.name: initialCapacity
params.javadoc: the initial capacity of the list. Must be non-negative.

throws.condition: if the specified initial capacity is negative.
if the requested array size exceeds the maximum array size

examples:
LongList list = new LongList(100);
list.size();       // returns 0 (capacity does not affect size)
list.isEmpty();    // returns true
new LongList(-1);  // throws IllegalArgumentException

constructors.signature: public LongList(final long[] a) throws IllegalArgumentException
constructors.javadoc_summary: Constructs a LongList backed by the specified array without copying it.

params.name: a
params.javadoc: the array whose elements are to be placed into this list.

throws.condition: if `a` is `null`

examples:
long[] a = {1L, 2L, 3L};
LongList list = new LongList(a);
list.size();         // returns 3
list.get(0);         // returns 1
a[0] = 99L;          // backing array is shared
list.get(0);         // returns 99
new LongList(null);  // throws IllegalArgumentException

constructors.signature: public LongList(final long[] a, final int size) throws IllegalArgumentException, IndexOutOfBoundsException
constructors.javadoc_summary: Constructs a LongList using the specified array as the internal storage with the specified size.

params.name: a
params.javadoc: the array to be used as the internal storage for this list.

params.name: size
params.javadoc: the number of elements in the list, must be between 0 and `a.length` (inclusive)

throws.condition: if `a` is `null` or if `size` is negative
if `size` is greater than the array length

examples:
long[] a = {1L, 2L, 3L, 4L};
LongList list = new LongList(a, 2);  // uses only the first 2 elements
list.size();                         // returns 2
list.get(1);                         // returns 2
new LongList(a, 5);                  // throws IndexOutOfBoundsException (size > a.length)

methods.name: range
methods.signature: public static LongList range(final long startInclusive, final long endExclusive) throws IllegalArgumentException

params.name: startInclusive
params.javadoc: the starting value (inclusive)

params.name: endExclusive
params.javadoc: the ending value (exclusive)

throws.condition: if the number of elements in the range exceeds `Integer.MAX_VALUE`.

methods.javadoc_summary: Creates a LongList containing an ascending sequence of long values in the range [`startInclusive`, `endExclusive`).
methods.returns: a new LongList containing the ascending sequence, or an empty list if `startInclusive >= endExclusive`
contract: If `startInclusive >= endExclusive`, an empty list is returned.
examples:
LongList.range(1, 5);  // returns [1, 2, 3, 4]
LongList.range(5, 1);  // returns []  (startInclusive >= endExclusive)
LongList.range(3, 3);  // returns []

methods.name: range
methods.signature: public static LongList range(final long startInclusive, final long endExclusive, final long by) throws IllegalArgumentException

params.name: startInclusive
params.javadoc: the starting value (inclusive)

params.name: endExclusive
params.javadoc: the ending value (exclusive)

params.name: by
params.javadoc: the step value for incrementing. Must not be zero.

throws.condition: if `by` is zero, or if the number of elements in the range exceeds `Integer.MAX_VALUE`.

methods.javadoc_summary: Creates a LongList containing a sequence of long values in the specified range with the given step.
methods.returns: a new LongList containing the sequence of values
contract: The sequence starts at startInclusive and increments by the step value until the value would reach or exceed endExclusive (or reach or fall below it if the step is negative).
examples:
LongList.range(0, 10, 2);   // returns [0, 2, 4, 6, 8]
LongList.range(10, 0, -2);  // returns [10, 8, 6, 4, 2]
LongList.range(1, 10, 3);   // returns [1, 4, 7]

params.name: startInclusive
params.javadoc: the starting value (inclusive)

params.name: endInclusive
params.javadoc: the ending value (inclusive)

throws.condition: if the number of elements in the range exceeds `Integer.MAX_VALUE`.

methods.javadoc_summary: Creates a LongList containing an ascending sequence of long values in the closed range [`startInclusive`, `endInclusive`].
methods.returns: a new LongList containing the ascending sequence, or an empty list if `startInclusive > endInclusive`
contract: If `startInclusive > endInclusive`, an empty list is returned.
examples:
LongList.rangeClosed(1, 4);  // returns [1, 2, 3, 4]
LongList.rangeClosed(4, 1);  // returns []  (startInclusive > endInclusive)
LongList.rangeClosed(3, 3);  // returns [3]

methods.name: rangeClosed
methods.signature: public static LongList rangeClosed(final long startInclusive, final long endInclusive, final long by) throws IllegalArgumentException

params.name: startInclusive
params.javadoc: the starting value (inclusive)

params.name: endInclusive
params.javadoc: the ending value (inclusive)

params.name: by
params.javadoc: the step value for incrementing. Must not be zero.

throws.condition: if `by` is zero, or if the number of elements in the range exceeds `Integer.MAX_VALUE`.

methods.javadoc_summary: Creates a LongList containing a sequence of long values in the specified closed range with the given step.
methods.returns: a new LongList containing the sequence of values
contract: The sequence starts at startInclusive and increments by the step value until the value would exceed endInclusive (or fall below it if step is negative).
The end value is included if it's exactly reachable by the step increments.
examples:
LongList.rangeClosed(0, 10, 2);   // returns [0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10]
LongList.rangeClosed(10, 0, -2);  // returns [10, 8, 6, 4, 2, 0]
LongList.rangeClosed(1, 10, 3);   // returns [1, 4, 7, 10]

methods.name: random
methods.signature: public static LongList random(final int length) throws NegativeArraySizeException

params.name: length
params.javadoc: the number of random elements to generate. Must be non-negative.

throws.condition: if `length` is negative

methods.javadoc_summary: Creates a LongList filled with random long values.
methods.returns: a new LongList containing random long values
contract: The values are not cryptographically secure; callers that need unpredictable values should use java.security.SecureRandom directly (for example, fill an array from it and wrap the array with `of(..)`).
examples:
LongList list = LongList.random(5);
list.size();          // returns 5 (values are unpredictable longs)
LongList.random(0);   // returns []
LongList.random(-1);  // throws NegativeArraySizeException

params.name: e
params.javadoc: the long value to be appended to this list

throws.condition: if the required capacity exceeds the maximum supported array size or the backing array cannot be enlarged

methods.javadoc_summary: Appends the specified element to the end of this list.
contract: The list will automatically grow if necessary to accommodate the new element.
If the internal array needs to be resized to accommodate the new element, all existing elements will be copied to a new, larger array.
examples:
LongList list = new LongList();
list.add(1L);  // list is now [1]
list.add(2L);  // list is now [1, 2]
list.size();   // returns 2

methods.name: add
methods.signature: public void add(final int index, final long e) throws IndexOutOfBoundsException, OutOfMemoryError

params.name: index
params.javadoc: the index at which the specified element is to be inserted

params.name: e
params.javadoc: the long value to be inserted

methods.javadoc_summary: Inserts the specified element at the specified position in this list.
contract: Shifts the element currently at that position (if any) and any subsequent elements to the right (adds one to their indices).
The list will automatically grow if necessary to accommodate the new element.
This method runs in linear time in the worst case (when inserting at the beginning of the list), as it may need to shift all existing elements.
examples:
LongList list = LongList.of(1L, 2L, 3L);
list.add(1, 99L);  // list is now [1, 99, 2, 3]
list.add(0, 0L);   // list is now [0, 1, 99, 2, 3]
list.add(5, 5L);   // list is now [0, 1, 99, 2, 3, 5] (insert at end)
list.add(7, 7L);   // throws IndexOutOfBoundsException

methods.javadoc_summary: Resolves a value from a nested map/collection structure using a dot-separated path.
methods.returns: the value at the specified path, or `null` if the path cannot be resolved
contract: If the path cannot be resolved (missing key, index out of bounds, or root map is `null`/empty), this method returns `null`.
If the path resolves to a `null` value, this method also returns `null`.
Use #getByPathIfExists(Map, String) when you need to distinguish "path exists with `null`" from "path cannot be resolved".

It is not reduced to the empty path: `getByPath(map, "")` reads the `""` key, while `getByPath(map, ".")` answers `null` (and `getByPathIfExists(map, ".")` answers `Nullable.empty()`) even when that key is present.
A segment is read as an index segment when it contains a `'['` and ends with a `']'`.
Its bracketed suffix must then match exactly `('[' [0-9]+ ']')+` - one or more groups of plain ASCII digits, running to the end of the segment.
Because `[...]` is reserved syntax, a map key that both contains a `'['` and ends with a `']'` - such as `"a[b]"` - is not addressable through a path, even when the map plainly contains it.
methods.performance: Indexing a non-java.util.List `Collection` is supported but walks the iterator, so it costs O(n) in the element position.

contract: For each key in the result map, the value is a pair where: If the key exists only in the first map, the pair contains the value from the first map and an empty Nullable If the key exists only in the second map, the pair contains an empty `Nullable` and the value from the second map If the key exists in both maps with different values, the pair contains both values Usage Examples: If either input map is `null`, it is treated as an empty map.

methods.signature: public static <K> void replaceKeys(final Map<K, ?> map, final Function<? super K, ? extends K> keyConverter) throws IllegalArgumentException, IllegalStateException, UnsupportedOperationException

params.name: map
params.javadoc: the map whose keys are to be replaced; modified in-place. If `null` or empty, no action is taken.

params.name: keyConverter
params.javadoc: the function applied once to each processed key to produce the new key; processing stops if conversion fails or produces a duplicate

throws.condition: if `keyConverter` is `null`.

if the converted keys contain duplicates (including multiple `null` values); the message identifies both original source keys without invoking the converter again. On the refill-in-place path, a map that cannot be cleared reports a duplicate this way only when two converted keys are the same reference (or both `null`) - a duplicate under any key equivalence - with the `UnsupportedOperationException` as the cause

if `map` does not support Map#clear() or Map#putAll(Map). Failures while applying the validated copy can leave the map empty or partially populated; only failures during conversion and duplicate detection leave it untouched. (On the refill-in-place path described above, any failure puts the original entries back.) When such a map cannot be cleared and two converted keys are merely `equals` - which an unmodifiable identity map would keep apart - this exception is thrown with that probable duplicate attached as a suppressed `IllegalStateException`

methods.javadoc_summary: Replaces (renames) the keys in the specified map by applying the given converter to each existing key.
contract: When a faithful scratch map can be built, this method operates in two phases: Validation phase: Computes the converted key for every current key and validates that no duplicates would be produced.
If duplicates are detected, throws IllegalStateException before modifying the map.

When no faithful scratch map can be built - a `Collections.synchronizedMap` or `checkedMap` wrapper, any other class that cannot be instantiated reflectively, or a BiMap (whose key and value map suppliers may impose comparator or identity semantics) - every key is still converted first, but duplicates are detected on `map` itself: it is cleared and refilled entry by entry in the original order, and on a duplicate (or any other failure while refilling) its original entries are put back, in their original order, before the exception propagates.

When such a map cannot even be cleared (an unmodifiable wrapper), the UnsupportedOperationException is reported - a duplicate is asserted only when it is certain under every key equivalence, see the `@throws` clauses below.
Notes: If a key converts to itself (i.e., `keyConverter.apply(key).equals(key)`), the entry is still removed and reinserted, which may affect iteration order in some map implementations.
If `keyConverter` returns `null`, it is treated as a valid key.
However, if `null` is returned for multiple keys, an IllegalStateException is thrown due to duplicate keys.
If the map is empty or `null`, this method returns immediately without any action.

methods.name: replaceKeys
methods.signature: public static <K, V> void replaceKeys(final Map<K, V> map, final Function<? super K, ? extends K> keyConverter, final BiFunction<? super V, ? super V, ? extends V> mergeFunction) throws IllegalArgumentException, UnsupportedOperationException

params.name: map
params.javadoc: the map whose keys are to be replaced; modified in-place. If `null` or empty, no action is taken.

params.name: keyConverter
params.javadoc: converts each existing key to its replacement key

params.name: mergeFunction
params.type: BiFunction<? super V, ? super V, ? extends V>
params.javadoc: merges values when multiple entries map to the same converted key. The function receives `(existingValue, incomingValue)` and returns the merged value. If it returns `null`, the entry is removed.

throws.condition: if any of `keyConverter`, `mergeFunction` is `null`.

if `map` does not support Map#clear() or Map#putAll(Map). Failures while applying the validated copy can leave the map empty or partially populated. Conversion failures leave the map untouched. Merging also precedes mutation when a faithful scratch copy is available; otherwise it runs on the cleared map, and a failure triggers restoration of the original entries as described above.

methods.javadoc_summary: Replaces (renames) keys in the specified map by applying the given converter, merging values when multiple original keys map to the same converted key.
contract: If that map already contains the converted key (according to the map implementation's own key semantics), `mergeFunction` combines the existing value (first argument) and incoming value (second argument).

When no faithful scratch map can be built (a `Collections.synchronizedMap` wrapper or a BiMap, for example), the keys are converted first and the entries are then folded directly into the cleared `map`, under its own key equivalence; any failure while folding - `mergeFunction` throwing included - puts the original entries back before the exception propagates.
When multiple keys convert to the same new key, merges occur in that iteration order.
If `keyConverter` returns `null` for any key, behavior depends on the map implementation.

If `mergeFunction` returns `null`, the entry accumulated so far under that converted key is removed - the same rule Map#merge(Object, Object, BiFunction) and #zip(Iterable, Iterable, BiFunction, IntFunction) follow.
A key is therefore missing from the result only when its last collision resolved to `null`.
Return a sentinel value and strip it afterwards when a dropped key must stay dropped.

Unlike Map#merge(Object, Object, BiFunction), `mergeFunction` is invoked based on key presence: it is called even when the existing value under the new key, or the value being moved, is `null` (the corresponding argument is then `null`).
If the map is empty or `null`, this method returns immediately without any action.

types.javadoc_summary: Finds the median element (or the two middle elements) of an array, a collection, or a range of either, without modifying the input.

methods.name: of
methods.signature: public static Pair<Character, OptionalChar> of(final char... source) throws IllegalArgumentException

params.name: source
params.javadoc: the array of characters to find the median from. Must not be `null` or empty.

throws.condition: if the specified array is `null` or empty.

methods.javadoc_summary: Finds the median value(s) from an array of characters using natural ordering.
methods.returns: a `Pair` containing the median value(s). For odd-length arrays, the `left` contains the median and `right` is empty. For even-length arrays, the `left` contains the smaller median and `right` contains the larger median.
contract: The median represents the middle value(s) when the array elements are arranged in sorted order.
For arrays with an odd number of elements, returns the single median value in the `left` component of the pair, with the `right` component empty.
For arrays with an even number of elements, returns the two median values, with the smaller value in the `left` component and the larger value in the `right` component.
methods.performance: Arrays of four or more elements are copied and the copy is sorted in O(n log n) time; shorter arrays are selected directly.
examples:
Pair<Character, OptionalChar> median = Median.of('z', 'a', 'm');

methods.name: hashCode
methods.signature: @Override public int hashCode()
methods.javadoc_summary: Returns the hash code value for this Multimap.
methods.returns: the hash code value for this Multimap
contract: Deciding equality some other way breaks the guarantee even when Map#hashCode() is implemented exactly as specified, because that hash code is built from `key.hashCode()`: two multimaps backed by java.util.TreeMaps that share one comparator inconsistent with `equals` can compare equal in both directions and still report different hash codes - under `String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER`, `A=[1]` and `a=[1]` hash to 97 and 65 - and so can an java.util.IdentityHashMap-backed multimap compared with a HashMap-backed one.

methods.returns: `true` if the specified object is equal to this Multimap, `false` otherwise
contract: Returns `true` if the specified object is also a Multimap and both have identical key-value collection mappings.
Note: Equality is delegated to the backing maps, so the value-collection types must also match: a `List` value collection never equals a `Set` value collection.
Consequently a nonempty ListMultimap and a nonempty SetMultimap are never equal even when they hold the same logical key-to-elements mappings.

methods.javadoc_summary: Returns a view of the contents of this multiset, grouped into Entry instances, each providing an element and its count.
methods.returns: a set of entries representing the data of this multiset
contract: Each returned Entry is an immutable snapshot of an element and its count taken when the entry was produced, so its count does not track later changes to the multiset and never becomes zero.

A multiset whose backing map separates two elements that `equals` calls equal (an java.util.IdentityHashMap, say) can therefore yield two entries that are equal to each other when their counts also match - which the Set contract does not allow.
Iterating the view is unaffected and the view's size is correct; the loss only appears if the entries are copied into an `equals`-based set, as `new HashSet<>(entrySet())` would.

methods.signature: public Map<E, Integer> toMap() throws IllegalStateException

throws.condition: if the result map treats two distinct elements of this multiset as the same key, so that their counts would collapse into one entry.

methods.javadoc_summary: Converts the multiset to a map where keys are elements and values are their counts.
methods.returns: a map with the elements of this multiset as keys and their counts as values
contract: When that type cannot be instantiated reflectively (for example a `Collections.synchronizedMap` wrapper or an anonymous map class) the result falls back to the matching JDK map family where one is known (`IdentityHashMap`, `WeakHashMap` or `ConcurrentHashMap`, so identity keys stay apart) and otherwise to a LinkedHashMap; if the backing map separates elements that `equals` treats as equal and the result is such a `LinkedHashMap`, two of them would then collapse into one entry, and rather than silently lose a count this method throws.

throws.condition: if `supplier` is `null`.
if `supplier` returns `null` (even for an empty multiset), or a stored key is `null` and the supplied map rejects null-key insertion
if a stored key cannot be compared or inserted into the supplied map
if entries are copied and the supplied map does not support insertion

methods.javadoc_summary: Converts the multiset to a map created by the provided supplier function.
methods.returns: the map created by `supplier`, populated with the elements of this multiset as keys and their counts as values
contract: If that map treats two source elements as the same key, the later entry in source iteration order overwrites the earlier count; counts are not combined.
examples:

TreeMap<String, Integer> map = multiset.toMap(size -> new TreeMap<>());

methods.name: toMapSortedByOccurrences
methods.signature: @SuppressWarnings("rawtypes") public Map<E, Integer> toMapSortedByOccurrences() throws IllegalStateException

throws.condition: if the backing map's key equivalence is finer than `equals`/ `hashCode`, so that two distinct elements would collapse into one entry.

methods.javadoc_summary: Converts the multiset to a map sorted by occurrences in ascending order.
methods.returns: a new insertion-ordered map (a LinkedHashMap) whose iteration order is by ascending count; empty if this multiset is empty
contract: If this multiset's backing map draws finer distinctions than that (an java.util.IdentityHashMap, or a comparator that separates elements `equals` calls equal) two of its elements would collapse into a single entry; rather than return counts that do not sum to #sumOfOccurrences(), this throws.

Use #toMap() (which copies into the backing map's own type when that type can be instantiated reflectively, otherwise into the fallback map it documents, and throws only if that fallback would merge two elements), #toMap(IntFunction) with a map of the backing map's own key equivalence, or #entrySet() for such a multiset.
A coarser backing (for example `String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER`) already merged those elements when they were added, so it is unaffected.

methods.javadoc_summary: Compares this object to the specified object.
methods.returns: `true` if the objects represent the same float value; `false` otherwise
contract: The result is `true` if and only if the argument is not `null` and is a `MutableFloat` object that contains the same `float` value as this object.
The comparison is performed via Float#compare(float, float), so two float values are considered the same if and only if `Float.compare` returns `0` for them.

Note that in most cases, for two instances of class `MutableFloat`, `f1` and `f2`, the value of `f1.equals(f2)` is `true` if and only if `f1.floatValue() == f2.floatValue()` also has the value `true`.
However, there are two exceptions: If `f1` and `f2` both represent `Float.NaN`, then the `equals` method returns `true`, even though `Float.NaN==Float.NaN` has the value `false`.
If `f1` represents `+0.0f` while `f2` represents `-0.0f`, or vice versa, the `equals` test has the value `false`, even though `0.0f==-0.0f` has the value `true`.

contract: A `valuesToFind` `Set` with a non-`equals` rule (a `Comparator`-based `TreeSet`, an identity set,...) decides when `c` is not a `Set`, while #containsAll(Collection, Collection) always defers to the receiver.

When neither side is a `Set` and the probed side is a `List` (whose `contains` is plain `equals`), a large enough list is copied into a `HashSet` once, so two lists cost `O(n + m)` rather than `O(n * m)`; any other non-`Set` collection is scanned per probe.

params.name: c
params.javadoc: the collection from which the values should be removed.

params.name: valuesToRemove
params.javadoc: the iterable of values to be removed from the collection. Nothing is removed before the values have been read, so it may safely be `c` itself or a view backed by `c`.

methods.javadoc_summary: Removes all occurrences of the specified values from the given collection.
methods.returns: `true` if the collection changed as a result of this call, `false` otherwise.
contract: When `c` is a `Set` it decides what "the same element" means: the values are offered to it one by one, so a `Comparator`-based `TreeSet` or an identity set removes whatever its own rule matches.

A receiver that is neither a `List` nor a `Set` and hands out a new instance for the same element on each traversal (a transforming view such as Guava's `Collections2.transform`) loses exactly its matches when `valuesToRemove` is not a `Set`, or is an exact `HashSet`, `LinkedHashSet`, `TreeSet`, `ConcurrentSkipListSet` or IdentityHashSet.

With any other `Set` such a receiver may keep some matches, and one that also reorders or regroups its elements when they are removed may lose a non-matching element instead; wrap the values in a `new HashSet<>(..)` for such a receiver.
Other calls invoke the receiver's removal operations and propagate any UnsupportedOperationException; depending on the receiver, that exception may be thrown even when nothing matches.
methods.performance: For any other receiver the argument decides, exactly as Collection#removeAll(Collection) specifies and as #excludeAll(Collection, Collection) does: a `Set` argument is probed as-is so that it keeps its own rule, and any other `Collection` is hashed first, which matches by `equals`/`hashCode` and turns an O(n*m) scan into O(n+m).

methods.signature: public static char[] removeDuplicates(final char[] a, final int fromIndex, final int toIndex, final boolean isSorted) throws IndexOutOfBoundsException

params.name: a
params.javadoc: the array from which duplicates should be removed, may be `null` or empty

params.name: fromIndex
params.javadoc: the initial index of the range to be considered for duplicate removal, inclusive

params.name: toIndex
params.javadoc: the final index of the range to be considered for duplicate removal, exclusive

params.name: isSorted
params.javadoc: `true` if the input array within the specified range is sorted (enables faster algorithm), `false` otherwise. With `true` only adjacent duplicates are removed, so equal elements must be adjacent; non-adjacent duplicates of an unsorted range are kept

throws.condition: if `fromIndex < 0` or `toIndex > a.length` or `fromIndex > toIndex`

methods.javadoc_summary: Removes duplicate elements from the specified range of the array.
methods.returns: a new array with distinct elements within the specified range, preserving order of first occurrence. Returns an empty array if the input is `null` or empty.
methods.performance: Algorithm: If `isSorted` is true: Uses optimized sequential comparison - O(n) time, O(n) space If `isSorted` is false: Keeps the first occurrence of each value using a fixed 8 KB bitmap of the 65536 possible `char` values (a range of at most 32 elements is compared with the values kept so far instead) - O(n) time, where `n` is the size of the requested range (`toIndex - fromIndex`), not the length of the whole array Performance Tip: If your array is sorted (or you can sort it first), pass `isSorted=true` for better performance with improved cache locality.

methods.javadoc_summary: Removes duplicate elements from the given collection.
methods.returns: `true` if the collection changed as a result of this call, `false` otherwise.
contract: When `isSorted` is `true`, elements equal under this rule must be adjacent.

Other collections are deduplicated through their iterator's `remove()` (`isSorted == true`, or two elements), or - when that is unsupported, as for a `Multiset`, or `isSorted` is `false` - re-populated with their distinct elements.
If that re-population fails part-way, the original content is restored on a best-effort basis before the failure propagates.
If restoration also fails, the collection may be empty or partially populated; a distinct restoration failure is suppressed.

methods.javadoc_summary: Moves a specified range of characters within a string to a new position.
methods.returns: a new string with the specified range moved to the new position; returns `null` for a `null` String after successful validation, which requires `(0, 0, 0)`, or an empty String if `str` is empty
contract: The newPositionAfterMove parameter indicates where the start of the moved range should be positioned in the resulting string.
examples:
// Moving a range of characters
N.moveRange("ABCDEFGH", 2, 5, 0);     // returns "CDEABFGH" (moves "CDE" to position 0)
N.moveRange("ABCDEFGH", 2, 5, 5);     // returns "ABFGHCDE" (moves "CDE" to position 5)
N.moveRange("Hello World", 0, 5, 6);  // returns " WorldHello" (moves "Hello" to position 6)

// Edge cases
N.moveRange((String) null, 0, 0, 0);  // returns null
N.moveRange("", 0, 0, 0);             // returns ""
N.moveRange("ABC", 1, 1, 1);          // returns "ABC" (no change when fromIndex == toIndex)
N.moveRange("ABC", 0, 2, 0);          // returns "ABC" (no change when already at position)

methods.name: retainAll
methods.signature: public static <T> boolean retainAll(final Collection<T> c, final Collection<? extends T> objsToKeep) throws UnsupportedOperationException

params.name: c
params.javadoc: the collection to be modified.

params.name: objsToKeep
params.javadoc: the collection containing elements to be retained in the first collection.

throws.condition: if `c` is non-empty and does not support the `clear` operation (when `objsToKeep` is `null` or empty) or the `retainAll` operation

methods.javadoc_summary: Retains only the elements in the specified collection that are present in the specified collection of elements to keep.
methods.returns: `true` if the first collection changed as a result of the call
contract: Note: if `objsToKeep` is `null` or empty ("keep nothing"), a non-empty input collection is cleared and `true` is returned.

Usage Examples: Membership rule: when `objsToKeep` is a `Set` it is passed to Collection#retainAll(Collection) unchanged, so that `Set`'s own notion of membership (a `Comparator`-based `TreeSet`, an identity set,...) decides what is kept.
Non-set arguments are snapshotted before modifying `c`, so a list or sublist backed by `c` retains the elements that were present in the argument when this method was called.
methods.performance: Any other `Collection` is copied into a `HashSet` first, at every size - which is equivalent for elements with a well-behaved `equals`/`hashCode` pair, and turns an O(n*m) scan into O(n+m), as #removeAll(Collection, Iterable) does.

N.sumDouble(new Double[] {1.5, 2.5, 3.0});  // returns 7.0

N.sumDouble(new Double[] {});               // returns 0.0

params.name: keyExtractor

throws.condition: if the array is `null` or empty, or if `keyExtractor` is `null`.

methods.javadoc_summary: Returns the minimum element from the array based on the key extracted by the `keyExtractor` function.
methods.returns: the minimum element based on the extracted key; may be `null` if the selected element is itself `null` (for example, when every element is `null` and `keyExtractor` tolerates `null`)
contract: If there are multiple smallest elements, the first one will be returned.
Null keys are considered to be maximum (placed last when comparing); a `null` element is not special-cased.

Note: `keyExtractor` is applied to the elements themselves, a `null` element included (except for a single-element input, where no comparison is made), so it must tolerate `null` if the input may contain `null`; otherwise the call fails with whatever the extractor throws.
It can be the minimum when all non-null keys are `NaN`.

`keyExtractor` is applied at most once per element position (at most `n` calls for `n >= 2` elements - fewer when an element is the same instance as the one before it or as the current candidate - and none for a single element), and the current candidate is always compared under the key it was selected with.

params.name: a
params.javadoc: the array of values, must not be `null` or empty

throws.condition: if the array is `null` or empty, or if `keyExtractor` is `null`.

methods.javadoc_summary: Returns the maximum element from the array based on the key extracted by the `keyExtractor` function.
methods.returns: the maximum element based on the extracted key; may be `null` if the selected element is itself `null` (for example, when every element is `null` and `keyExtractor` tolerates `null`)
contract: If there are multiple largest elements, the first one will be returned.
Null keys are considered to be minimum (placed first when comparing); a `null` element is not special-cased.

Note: `keyExtractor` is applied to the elements themselves, a `null` element included (except for a single-element input, where no comparison is made), so it must tolerate `null` if the input may contain `null`; otherwise the call fails with whatever the extractor throws.

`keyExtractor` is applied at most once per element position (at most `n` calls for `n >= 2` elements - fewer when an element is the same instance as the one before it or as the current candidate - and none for a single element), and the current candidate is always compared under the key it was selected with.

methods.returns: the median in the specified array; `null` if the median element is itself `null`
contract: Null values are considered to be minimum (placed first when comparing).
The median is the middle value when the elements are sorted in ascending order.
For array with an odd number of elements, this is the exact middle element.
For array with an even number of elements, this method returns the lower of the two middle elements (not the average).
When several elements compare equal at the selection boundary, which of them are returned is unspecified (it can depend on the presence of `null` elements in the range).
examples:

N.lowerMedian(new Integer[] {5, 2, 8, 1});     // returns 2 (lower of two middles of sorted {1,2,5,8})
N.lowerMedian(new Integer[] {});               // throws IllegalArgumentException (empty array)

methods.javadoc_summary: Returns the median value of all elements in the specified array.
methods.returns: the median in the specified array; `null` if the median element is itself `null`
contract: The median is the middle value when the elements are sorted in ascending order.
For array with an odd number of elements, this is the exact middle element.
For array with an even number of elements, this method returns the lower of the two middle elements (not the average).

When several elements compare equal at the lower-median rank, this overload prefers the element currently at index `a.length - (a.length / 2 + 1)` if that element compares equal to the `kthLargest` selection.
If the range may contain `null`, `comparator` must accept `null` (as the default `null`-first ordering does); otherwise the comparator's own exception propagates.
When several elements compare equal at the selection boundary, which of them are returned is unspecified (it can depend on the presence of `null` elements in the range).
examples:
String[] a = {"zebra", "apple", "mango"};
N.lowerMedian(a, Comparator.naturalOrder());                                                 // returns "mango" (middle of sorted {apple, mango, zebra}; odd count)
N.lowerMedian(new String[] {"zebra", "apple", "mango", "kiwi"}, Comparator.naturalOrder());  // returns "kiwi" (lower of the two middle values "kiwi" and "mango"; even count)
N.lowerMedian(new String[] {}, Comparator.naturalOrder());                                   // throws IllegalArgumentException (empty array)

methods.javadoc_summary: Returns the median value of all elements in the specified collection.
methods.returns: the median in the specified collection; `null` if the median element is itself `null`
contract: The median is the middle value when the elements are sorted in ascending order.
For collection with an odd number of elements, this is the exact middle element.
For collection with an even number of elements, this method returns the lower of the two middle elements (not the average).

When several elements compare equal at the lower-median rank, this overload prefers the element currently at index `c.size() - (c.size() / 2 + 1)` if that element compares equal to the `kthLargest` selection.
If the range may contain `null`, `comparator` must accept `null` (as the default `null`-first ordering does); otherwise the comparator's own exception propagates.
When several elements compare equal at the selection boundary, which of them are returned is unspecified (it can depend on the presence of `null` elements in the range).
examples:
List<String> c = Arrays.asList("zebra", "apple", "mango");
N.lowerMedian(c, Comparator.naturalOrder());                                                 // returns "mango" (middle of sorted {apple, mango, zebra}; odd count)
N.lowerMedian(Arrays.asList("zebra", "apple", "mango", "kiwi"), Comparator.naturalOrder());  // returns "kiwi" (lower of the two middle values "kiwi" and "mango"; even count)
N.lowerMedian(N.<String> emptyList(), Comparator.naturalOrder());                            // throws IllegalArgumentException (empty collection)

params.name: a
params.javadoc: the array to iterate

params.name: fromIndex
params.javadoc: the starting index (inclusive) of the range

params.name: toIndex
params.javadoc: the ending index (exclusive) of the range; if `fromIndex > toIndex`, iterates in reverse order, from `fromIndex` down to, but excluding, `toIndex`. If `fromIndex` equals the array length, reverse iteration starts at the last element. In reverse mode `toIndex` may be `-1`; passing `-1` is the only way to include element 0 in a reverse iteration, and `(-1, -1)` is an empty range (the reverse idiom `(length - 1, -1)` applied to an empty input)

params.name: action
params.javadoc: the action to execute, receiving index and element

throws.condition: in forward mode (`fromIndex <= toIndex`) if `fromIndex < 0` or `toIndex > a.length`; in reverse mode if `toIndex < -1` or `fromIndex > a.length` (a `null` array is treated as length `0`)
if `action` is `null`.
if the action throws an exception

methods.javadoc_summary: Executes the action for each element in the specified range of the array with its index.

methods.javadoc_summary: Executes commands asynchronously using the default executor and returns an iterator for lazy result iteration.
methods.returns: an iterator that yields one `null` per completed command, in completion order. The caller should fully exhaust the iterator: advancing it is what drives completion handling and surfaces any command failure (see the note above).
contract: If an error occurs in a command, iteration is interrupted and the error is thrown.
If the waiting thread is interrupted, `hasNext()` throws and the interrupt status is restored.
A command's failure is re-thrown when that command's completion is reached; if the iterator is not fully exhausted, failures of not-yet-observed commands are never surfaced.
Commands that have already started are not canceled when iteration stops early, and abandoning the iterator leaves them running.

types.javadoc_summary: Static utilities for numeric conversion, parsing, formatting, rounding, comparison, integer arithmetic, combinatorics, statistics, and selected mathematical functions.

methods.name: convert
methods.signature: @MayReturnNull public static <T extends Number> T convert(final Number value, final Class<? extends T> targetType) throws IllegalArgumentException, NumberFormatException, ArithmeticException

params.name: value
params.javadoc: the number to convert

params.name: targetType
params.javadoc: the class object representing the target type

throws.condition: if `targetType` is `null`, or if, for a non-null `value`, `targetType` is not a supported conversion target — that is, it is neither one of the built-in numeric conversions nor a `Number` type with a public `String` factory method or constructor (for example `Number` itself, or any other abstract `Number` subtype)

if a conversion routed through the target type's string parser cannot parse the source's string form; the message embeds only a bounded, escaped preview of that form, as every other parse failure reported by this class does

if the conversion to an integer (`byte`/`short`/`int`/`long`) target would overflow, including a `NaN`/`±Infinity` input; or if a `NaN`/`±Infinity` value is converted to a `BigInteger` or `BigDecimal` target (a `float`/`double` target saturates to `±Infinity` instead of throwing); or if a `BigInteger` result exceeds the JDK implementation's supported magnitude, as `convert(new BigDecimal("1e2147483647"), BigInteger.class)` does (a `BigDecimal` target does not need to expand that scale into an integer)

methods.javadoc_summary: Converts the given number to the specified target type with overflow checking.
methods.returns: the converted number as an instance of the target type, or the default value of the target type if the input value is null; a `null` value takes that default without `targetType` being checked for usability, so `convert(null, Number.class)` is `null`
contract: If a conversion to an integer type would overflow, an `ArithmeticException` is thrown; a `float`/`double` target instead saturates to `±Infinity` (IEEE-754 semantics).

For an integral or arbitrary-precision target its value is recovered from its canonical decimal text when it has one and otherwise from its `doubleValue()`, because `longValue()` is allowed to wrap for such a type.
The `float`/`double` targets never read the text, so they can recover a different source value when the subtype's text and numeric accessors disagree.

The opposite direction is a plain IEEE-754 narrowing (`floatValue()`, ties to even), as in #toFloat(Object): the shortest decimal spelling of a `double` already narrows to the same `float` as the value itself except when the value is exactly halfway between two floats, so a decimal round trip there would only require parsing and can break ties-to-even.
examples:
// A fractional value is truncated toward zero, then range-checked
Integer result = Numbers.convert(123.45, Integer.class);                              // returns 123
Long longValue = Numbers.convert(new BigInteger("9223372036854775807"), Long.class);  // returns 9223372036854775807L
Double widened = Numbers.convert(7, Double.class);                                    // returns 7.0

// Edge cases: null yields the target type's default; an out-of-range or non-finite
// value throws for an integer/BigInteger target but saturates for float/double
Byte byteValue = Numbers.convert(null, Byte.class);      // returns null
byte primByteValue = Numbers.convert(null, byte.class);  // returns 0
Numbers.convert(1000, Byte.class);                       // throws ArithmeticException (outside byte range)
Numbers.convert(Double.NaN, Integer.class);              // throws ArithmeticException (not representable)
Float saturated = Numbers.convert(1e300, Float.class);   // returns Infinity (IEEE-754 saturation)
Numbers.convert(1, Number.class);                        // throws IllegalArgumentException (unusable target type)
Numbers.convert(null, Number.class);                     // returns null (a null value is never checked against the target)

Numbers.extractFirstInt("price: $45.99");  // returns OptionalInt.of(45)
Numbers.extractFirstInt("total: -10");     // returns OptionalInt.of(-10)

// Edge cases
Numbers.extractFirstInt("no numbers");      // returns OptionalInt.empty()
Numbers.extractFirstInt("-.5");             // returns OptionalInt.of(5) (the sign is skipped: it does not touch the digits)
Numbers.extractFirstInt("");                // returns OptionalInt.empty()
Numbers.extractFirstInt(null);              // returns OptionalInt.empty()
Numbers.extractFirstInt("id=99999999999");  // throws NumberFormatException (a matched token outside int range)

methods.javadoc_summary: Checks whether the String matches the Numbers-supported numeric grammar accepted by #createNumber(String).

methods.name: createNumber
methods.signature: @MayReturnNull public static Number createNumber(final String str) throws NumberFormatException, ArithmeticException

params.name: str
params.javadoc: the string to convert; `null` or empty returns `null`

throws.condition: if the non-empty string cannot be converted
if an arbitrary-precision result exceeds the JDK implementation's supported magnitude

methods.javadoc_summary: Converts a `String` to a `Number`.
methods.returns: the parsed Number value, or `null` if the input string is `null` or empty
contract: If the string starts with an optional sign (`+` or `-`) followed by `0x` (lower or upper case) or `#`, it is parsed as a signed hexadecimal value and returned as the narrowest supported type whose inclusive bounds contain that value: `Integer`, then `Long`, otherwise `BigInteger`.

If it is found, a larger type is used when the requested type overflows to infinity or underflows to a signed zero while the input still contains non-zero digits (`"1e-50f"` is a `Double`, not a `Float`).
If a type specifier is not found, integral forms try `Integer` then `Long` then `BigInteger`.
A finite, nonzero `Double` is kept even when the decimal does not survive IEEE-754 rounding: `"1.0000000000000000000000001"` returns `Double.valueOf(1.0)`, not a `BigDecimal`.
examples:
Numbers.createNumber("123");                          // returns Integer
Numbers.createNumber("123.45");                       // returns Double
Numbers.createNumber("123L");                         // returns Long
Numbers.createNumber("123.45f");                      // returns Float
Numbers.createNumber("0xFF");                         // returns Integer (255)
Numbers.createNumber("-0x80000000");                  // returns Integer (-2147483648)
Numbers.createNumber("010");                          // returns Integer (8, octal; toInt("010") is 10)
Numbers.createNumber("1.0000000000000000000000001");  // returns Double 1.0 (IEEE-754 rounding)

// Edge cases
Numbers.createNumber(null);     // returns null
Numbers.createNumber("");       // returns null
Numbers.createNumber("0xFFL");  // throws NumberFormatException (use decodeLong)
Numbers.createNumber(" ");      // throws NumberFormatException
Numbers.createNumber("\n");     // throws NumberFormatException
Numbers.createNumber("abc");    // throws NumberFormatException
Numbers.createNumber("1٢11");   // throws NumberFormatException (non-ASCII digit)

methods.javadoc_summary: Returns the least common multiple (LCM) of two integers.
methods.returns: the least common multiple of the absolute values of `a` and `b`; returns `0` if either is zero
contract: Usage Examples: Special cases: The invocations `Numbers.lcm(Integer.MIN_VALUE, n)` and `Numbers.lcm(n, Integer.MIN_VALUE)` throw an `ArithmeticException` for every non-zero `n`, because once an operand is `-2^31` the true LCM is at least 2^31, which is too large for an int value (the smallest such case is when `Math.abs(n)` is a power of 2, where the result would be exactly 2^31).
examples:
Numbers.lcm(4, 6);    // returns 12
Numbers.lcm(3, 7);    // returns 21  (coprime numbers: lcm equals product)
Numbers.lcm(12, 18);  // returns 36
Numbers.lcm(-4, 6);   // returns 12  (sign-independent)

// Edge cases
Numbers.lcm(65536, 65536 * 2);      // returns 131072
Numbers.lcm(0, 5);                  // returns 0
Numbers.lcm(0, 0);                  // returns 0
Numbers.lcm(Integer.MIN_VALUE, 2);  // throws ArithmeticException (the true lcm is 2^31)
Numbers.lcm(46341, 46341 * 2 - 1);  // throws ArithmeticException (the product exceeds int range)

params.name: values

throws.condition: if `values` is `null` or empty.

methods.javadoc_summary: Returns the arithmetic mean of `values`.
methods.returns: the arithmetic mean of the values
contract: If these values are a sample drawn from a population, this is also an unbiased estimator of the arithmetic mean of the population.

The result is not guaranteed to be the correctly rounded mean: the exact integral total is converted to `double` before the division, so once it exceeds 253 in magnitude the result can be one ulp off even when the exact mean is representable — `mean(18014398509481986L, 0L, 0L)` is `6.004799503160661E15`, whereas the exact mean is `6004799503160662`.
examples:
Numbers.mean(1L, 2L, 3L, 4L, 5L);     // returns 3.0
Numbers.mean(new long[] {10L, 20L});  // returns 15.0
Numbers.mean(-10L, 0L, 10L);          // returns 0.0

// Edge cases
Numbers.mean(5L);                              // returns 5.0 (a single value)
Numbers.mean(Long.MAX_VALUE, Long.MAX_VALUE);  // returns 9.223372036854776E18 (no wrap: computed without an overflowing intermediate sum)
Numbers.mean(Long.MIN_VALUE, Long.MIN_VALUE);  // returns -9.223372036854776E18
Numbers.mean(new long[0]);                     // throws IllegalArgumentException (no values)
Numbers.mean((long[]) null);                   // throws IllegalArgumentException

methods.signature: public static boolean fuzzyEquals(final float a, final float b, final float tolerance) throws IllegalArgumentException

params.name: a
params.javadoc: the first float value to compare

params.name: b
params.javadoc: the second float value to compare

params.name: tolerance
params.javadoc: the maximum absolute difference allowed between the two values to consider them equal; must be non-negative

throws.condition: if `tolerance` is `< 0` or NaN.

methods.javadoc_summary: Returns `true` if `a` and `b` are within `tolerance` of each other.
methods.returns: `true` if the absolute difference between `a` and `b` is less than or equal to `tolerance`, or if `a == b` (including equal infinities), or if both are NaN; `false` otherwise
contract: If `a == b`, then `a` and `b` are always fuzzily equal.
If `tolerance` is zero, and neither `a` nor `b` is NaN, then `a` and `b` are fuzzily equal if and only if `a == b`.
examples:
Numbers.fuzzyEquals(1.0001f, 1.0002f, 0.001f);  // returns true  (within tolerance)
Numbers.fuzzyEquals(1.0f, 1.1f, 0.01f);         // returns false (exceeds tolerance)

// Edge cases
Numbers.fuzzyEquals(0.0f, -0.0f, 0.0f);                     // returns true  (positive and negative zero are equal)
Numbers.fuzzyEquals(Float.NaN, Float.NaN, 0.1f);            // returns true  (all NaNs are fuzzily equal)
Numbers.fuzzyEquals(Float.NaN, 1.0f, 0.1f);                 // returns false (NaN equals only NaN)
Numbers.fuzzyEquals(1.0f, 1e20f, Float.POSITIVE_INFINITY);  // returns true  (infinite tolerance)
Numbers.fuzzyEquals(1.0f, 1.0f, -0.1f);                     // throws IllegalArgumentException (negative tolerance)

params.name: a
params.javadoc: the number on which to compute the inverse hyperbolic sine

methods.javadoc_summary: Computes the inverse hyperbolic sine (arcsinh) of a number.
methods.returns: the inverse hyperbolic sine of `a`
examples:
Numbers.asinh(1.0);   // returns ~0.88137
Numbers.asinh(-1.0);  // returns ~-0.88137
Numbers.asinh(10.0);  // returns ~2.99822

// Edge cases: the domain is all of the reals, so this method never throws
Numbers.asinh(0.0);                       // returns 0.0

methods.name: acosh
methods.signature: public static double acosh(final double a)

methods.javadoc_summary: Computes the inverse hyperbolic cosine (arccosh) of a number.
methods.returns: the inverse hyperbolic cosine of `a`, or NaN if `a < 1` or `a` is NaN
examples:
Numbers.acosh(2.0);   // returns ~1.31696

// Edge cases: outside the domain the result is NaN; this method never throws
Numbers.acosh(1.0);                       // returns 0.0 (the domain starts at 1)

methods.name: atanh
methods.signature: public static double atanh(final double a)

params.name: a
params.javadoc: the number on which to compute the inverse hyperbolic tangent

methods.javadoc_summary: Computes the inverse hyperbolic tangent (arctanh) of a number.
methods.returns: the inverse hyperbolic tangent of `a`; `±Infinity` at `±1`, `NaN` when `|a| > 1` or `a` is `NaN`
contract: Using `log1p` avoids loss of small values when adding them to one before taking a logarithm.
examples:
Numbers.atanh(0.5);   // returns ~0.54931
Numbers.atanh(-0.5);  // returns ~-0.54931
Numbers.atanh(0.9);   // returns ~1.47222

// Edge cases: outside the domain the result is NaN; this method never throws
Numbers.atanh(0.0);         // returns 0.0
Numbers.atanh(-0.0);        // returns -0.0 (signed zero is preserved)
Numbers.atanh(1.0);         // returns Double.POSITIVE_INFINITY
Numbers.atanh(-1.0);        // returns Double.NEGATIVE_INFINITY
Numbers.atanh(1.5);         // returns NaN (outside the domain)
Numbers.atanh(Double.NaN);  // returns NaN

methods.javadoc_summary: Returns an `ObjIterator` that defers creation of the underlying iterator until the first call to `hasNext()` or `next()`.
